articles.title: Watch: Mount Mayon volcano erupts for nearly 6 minutes in Philippines, spews ash 3 km high
articles.summary: A nearly six-minute explosive eruption at the Philippines’ Mount Mayon sent an ash column soaring 3,000 metres into the sky on Friday, prompting
articles.body: A nearly six-minute explosive eruption at the Philippines’ Mount Mayon sent an ash column soaring 3,000 metres into the sky on Friday, prompting authorities to raise the volcano’s alert level and order evacuations near its crater.The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) raised the alert level from 2 to 3 on its five-level scale and urged residents within a six-kilometre radius of the crater to evacuate. The ash column gradually drifted southwest towards nearby population centres. There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage.In its bulletin, the institute said Mayon had entered a new phase of magmatic eruption, increasing the possibility of lava flows and hazardous pyroclastic density currents (PDCs) along the upper and middle slopes of the volcano in the coming days and weeks.Authorities warned residents of the dangers posed by pyroclastic flows, lava, rockfalls and other volcanic hazards. Aircraft were also advised to avoid flying close to the volcano.Mayon among Philippines' most active volcanoesStanding at 2,462 metres, Mount Mayon is located about 330 km southeast of Manila and is known for its near-perfect cone. It is among three volcanoes in the Philippines that have shown elevated activity this year, although no major eruptions had been reported.The volcano has a history of forcing large-scale evacuations. In June 2023, more than 12,000 people living along its lower slopes were moved to evacuation centres amid concerns over ash emissions and toxic gases from its crater.Volcanic activity and earthquakes are common in the Philippines, which lies along the Pacific Ring of Fire, a region marked by the movement and collision of tectonic plates.The country's most powerful eruption in recent decades was that of Mount Pinatubo in 1991. articles.summary: Intel CFO David Zinsner has shared a warning on memory prices and shortage of key components saying that the company does not expect memory supply to
articles.body: Intel CFO David Zinsner has shared a warning on memory prices and shortage of key components saying that the company does not expect memory supply to improve in 2027. “Make no mistake, we are not optimistic about next year in terms of memory,” he said during Intel’s latest earnings call adding “we’ll, you know, have to see in ‘28 whether things improve, but our expectation is that it does not improve in ‘27.” His comments suggest that consumers may have to wait longer for relief from rising device prices.Intel says budget laptop chips are already sold outDuring the earnings call, Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said demand for the company’s budget-focused Wildcat Lake chips “is outstripping supply.”David Zinsner confirmed that the chips are now sold out. “We've seen significant growth in Wildcat Lake. It’s coming exactly at the right time because it’s cost-optimized and we’re seeing a lot of focus in that regard,” he said.Wildcat Lake chips are appearing in lower-cost Windows laptops, including the new Dell XPS 13 and HP OmniBook 5 14. These devices are positioned as more affordable options in a market where rising memory costs have put pressure on PC prices.However, some of these laptops start with just 8GB of RAM. articles.title: JOHN KOUFOS: Trump’s ‘Shield of the Americas’ could help defend us from cartels
articles.summary: Brazil's refusal to join the Trump's "Shield of the Americas" leaves an important gap in the hemispheric fight against the powerful and deadly drug cartels
articles.body: In my first career, I stood in courtrooms as a defense attorney dealing intimately with the fallout of organized crime and gang violence. I have cross-examined operatives, analyzed thousands of pages of gang intelligence and witnessed firsthand the brutal efficiency of transnational syndicates. If my time immersed in the legal trenches of the gang world taught me one undeniable truth, it is this: cartels do not respect international borders. In fact, they weaponize them. For too long, the jurisdictional lines on a map have served as the greatest defense strategy for the world's most violent criminal organizations. We have treated multinational, multibillion-dollar criminal enterprises as localized law enforcement problems. Fortunately, the landscape of international justice is shifting. The U.S.-led "Shield of the Americas" initiative, which recently designated eight major criminal groups as foreign terrorist organizations, is fundamentally rewriting the playbook on how we dismantle these syndicates. There remains one critical holdout, Brazil, whose president is not expected to join this critical coalition. Indeed, the re-election of incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva all but ensures an increase in organized criminal activity in Brazil. ICE ARRESTS MORE THAN 100 ALLEGED GANG MEMBERS IN SINGLE WEEK, INCLUDING VIOLENT MS-13, TDA SUSPECTS: DHS The reality of the modern syndicate To understand the necessity of this initiative, one must understand how modern cartels operate. In the courtroom, you quickly realize that the street-level gang members, like the MS-13 triggermen or the Tren de Aragua enforcers, can be the lowest rung on a massive, sophisticated corporate ladder. These organizations operate with the logistical precision of Fortune 500 companies. They manage complex supply chains, launder money through intricate global financial networks and employ specialized cells for enforcement, distribution and corruption. At times, our legal framework has been outmatched by their agility. A drug shipment might originate in the Andes, be financed through a front company in Central America and be distributed by local gangs in American cities. When law enforcement attempts to build a case, they can hit a variety of bureaucratic obstacles and challenges sharing evidence, securing extraditions or tracing illicit funds across different countries. The cartels know this and deliberately structure their operations to exploit operational disconnects between regional governments. EXCLUSIVE: FBI EXTRADITIONS SOAR AS PATEL RAMPS UP FOREIGN OUTREACH, VOWS 'NO SANCTUARY' The power of the terrorist designation By officially designating eight major cartels and gangs, including the Sinaloa cartel, the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG) and Tren de Aragua, as foreign terrorist organizations and specially designated global terrorists, the U.S. government dramatically altered the legal reality. RUBIO DESIGNATES ECUADORIAN GANG LINKED TO DRUG TRAFFICKING A TERRORIST GROUP The terrorist designation unlocks a completely different enforcement arsenal. It allows for the immediate freezing of assets, imposes severe penalties for anyone providing "material support" and authorizes deep, aggressive disruption of their financial networks. You cannot arrest your way out of a cartel problem — you must disrupt the business itself. By targeting their money and imposing serious consequences on the seemingly legitimate financial institutions that launder it, the Shield of the Americas strikes at the absolute core of cartel power. It equips law enforcement to fight proactively and focus on strategic dismantling of cartel financial infrastructure. DRUG CARTEL KINGPIN AMONG TARGETS IN SWEEPING TRUMP CRACKDOWN ON ALLEGED MEXICAN CORRUPTION NETWORK Hemispheric intelligence and military coordination Equally crucial is the initiative’s mandate for unprecedented intelligence sharing and military coordination. Currently, countries like Argentina, El Salvador, Peru, Ecuador, Panama, Paraguay and Chile are participating in the Shield of the Americas. EXCLUSIVE: TRUMP’S NEW SECURITY ALLIANCE FACES FIRST REAL-WORLD TEST DEEP IN SOUTH AMERICA AS TROOPS DEPLOY This will help break down silos where one law enforcement agency has one piece of the puzzle, while authorities in Colombia or El Salvador hold the rest. Without a streamlined mechanism to share that data, the kingpins remain untouchable. The Shield of the Americas facilitates the real-time sharing of actionable intelligence among partner nations. This means that a cartel operative’s communications intercepted in Lima could be instantly used to disrupt a trafficking route in Central America and ultimately support a federal indictment in New York. Furthermore, joint military coordination ensures that the sheer firepower of these cartels could be matched. When law enforcement attempts to build a case, they can hit a variety of bureaucratic obstacles and challenges sharing evidence, securing extraditions or tracing illicit funds across different countries. The Brazilian loophole The final critical piece of this initiative is Brazil, South America’s largest nation. CONSERVATIVE WAVE HITS ROADBLOCK IN BRAZIL AS LULA HOLDS OFF BOLSONARO CHALLENGE Brazil is a continent-sized nation with its own deeply entrenched criminal organizations, most notably the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and the Comando Vermelho. These groups have grown into major forces in the global drug trade, forging alliances with international cartels and expanding their reach far beyond Brazilian borders. Unfortunately, the current government has abstained from joining the U.S.-led effort, which is expected to continue in light of the recent presidential election. Brazil’s participation would have a tremendous impact. The cartels would lose one of their most significant safe havens and operational hubs in the hemisphere. A unified front stretching from the U.S.-Mexico border down to the Southern Cone would squeeze transnational syndicates from every direction. It would close the geographical and jurisdictional gaps they have exploited for generations. The human cost of cartel operations is staggering. Hundreds of thousands of American lives have been lost to cartel-linked fentanyl overdoses, while communities across Latin America have been destabilized by extreme violence and corruption. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The Shield of the Americas represents a profound modernization of our approach to international justice. By recognizing these cartels for the global terror threats they are, strangling their finances and uniting the hemisphere's law enforcement and military resources, we are finally fighting the battle on equal footing. The cartels have operated globally for decades. It is long past time the law did the same.

articles.title: Woman found fungus and visible contamination in a Rs 230 butter pack bought from a retail store; Hyderabad consumer commission has now ordered Rs 2 lakh in damages and compensation, and referred the matter to FSSAI for action
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Hyderabad has held a butter manufacturer and retailer guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A district consumer commission in Hyderabad has held a butter manufacturer and retailer guilty of deficiency in service and unfair trade practice after a woman found fungus and other visible contamination in a packet of organic cooking butter she had purchased from a retail outlet. The commission found that improper storage conditions had led to contamination of the product.The commission, in its October 9, 2026, order, directed the retailer and manufacturer to jointly refund Rs 230, pay Rs 1 lakh as compensation and Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs. It also imposed Rs 1 lakh as punitive damages, to be deposited in the consumer welfare fund, and referred the matter to the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) for necessary action.Fungus found in organic butter packAccording to the commission order, the complainant, Sandya Chavula, purchased a packet of Akshaya Kalpa Organic Cooking Butter for Rs 230 from a retail outlet in Sainikpuri, Secunderabad, on January 28, 2025. The product had been manufactured on December 21, 2024, and was due to expire on April 19, 2025.When she opened the packet at home, she found fungus and other visible contamination in the butter, making it unfit for consumption. She returned to the store and complained about the product. She alleged that the staff behaved and threatened her.The complainant also approached the manufacturer, which asked her to take up the issue with the retailer. She then sent a legal notice to the manufacturer and concerned authorities, including FSSAI and the National Dairy Development Board, on March 11, 2025.The manufacturer, in its reply dated March 17, 2025, attributed the problem to improper storage at the retail outlet. It said the temperature in the retailer's cold chain was 3-4 degrees above the recommended level and that the open chiller being used could not maintain the required temperature.What did the retailer and manufacturer say?The retailer contended that it had sold the product in the sealed condition in which it received it from the supplier. It said it had no role in the manufacture, packaging or marketing of the butter and denied responsibility for the alleged contamination.The manufacturer said its representatives and an expert committee had inspected the outlet, the product and its cold-storage facilities after receiving the complaint. It claimed that the inspection found that the storage temperature was not in line with the product's specifications and that the store staff were advised on the required precautions.It denied any deficiency in service or unfair trade practice, arguing that the reports relied on by the complainant did not establish the condition of the product at the time of purchase.Commission's findingA bench comprising president Vakkanti Narasimha Rao and members P.V.T.R. Jawahar Babu and Suma Vala said the manufacturer's reply to the legal notice was significant because it pointed to shortcomings in the storage arrangements at the retail outlet.The commission noted that the manufacturer had itself stated that an open chiller could not maintain the recommended temperature and that the product needed to be stored in a closed chiller below 4 degrees Celsius. It had also suggested that the retailer use the manufacturer's closed chillers and train its staff in maintaining the cold chain.The commission said the manufacturer's reply showed that both parties had failed to take adequate preventive measures. While the retailer did not maintain the required storage temperature, the manufacturer failed to ensure that the storage conditions were suitable before placing the product for sale.It also referred to the manufacturer's butter analysis log book, which matched the batch number D19L07 and the manufacturing date of December 21, 2024, with the product sold to the complainant on January 28, 2025."The product sold to the complainant was contaminated and adulterated, which could be harmful if consumed without noticing the contamination," the commission noted.The commission held that selling the contaminated product amounted to an unfair trade practice. It also directed that the matter be referred to FSSAI under Section 90 of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, for appropriate action."The opposite parties have failed to take necessary precautions to ensure that the product is stored in proper conditions and is safe for consumption," it further added.Final orderThe commission partly allowed the complaint and directed the opposite parties to:Jointly and severally refund Rs 230 to the complainant.Pay Rs 50,000 each, totalling Rs 1 lakh, as compensation for mental agony and inconvenience.Pay Rs 10,000 towards litigation costs.Deposit punitive damages of Rs 50,000 each, totalling Rs 1 lakh, into the consumer welfare fund maintained by the commission.Discontinue the unfair and restrictive trade practice under Section 39(1)(g) of the Consumer Protection Act.The commission also directed that the matter be referred to the deputy director of FSSAI's Hyderabad branch for necessary action under Section 90 of the Act.The directions have to be complied with within 45 days of receipt of the order.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia reports interception of Houthi drone targeting Mecca
articles.summary: Houthis deny targeting the region of the Muslim holy city as hostilities continue to escalate.
articles.body:
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen has reported that it intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s Mecca region .

The drone was “intercepted and destroyed” on Friday morning, coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said in a social media post. It was also reported that a missile aimed at western Saudi Arabia was earlier brought down, as hostilities between the Riyadh-backed Yemen government and Iran-backed Houthis continue to escalate .

A Houthi spokesperson denied targeting the Muslim holy city or surrounding region, reiterating that the group’s cross-border attacks remain strictly focused on Saudi energy and military infrastructure.

The Saudi-led coalition has previously accused the Houthis of launching drones towards Islam’s two holiest cities: Mecca and Medina .

“Our operations target [Saudi] oil facilities and military bases, and there is no longer anyone in this world who believes these fabrications and lies propagated by the criminal Al Saud regime,” the Houthi spokesman wrote.

The opposing claims come as hostilities continue with no sign of slowing , and humanitarian agencies warn of worsening conditions for civilians.

On Thursday, the Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the kingdom’s eastern region. It later said two ballistic missiles launched towards the Saudi capital, Riyadh, were also intercepted and destroyed.

Al-Malki reported early on Friday that the coalition’s air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi cruise missile that targeted western Saudi Arabia.

Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported later that coalition air attacks were targeting the Mahliyah district in Marib, Haifan in Taiz , and Huwaishan in al-Jawf in the country.

Al Jazeera Arabic’s Hadeel al-Yamani reported from Taiz that fighting along the front lines was persisting.

The governor of Taiz said the city was suffering heavy shelling, with residential neighbourhoods taking hits.

“Aircraft can be heard frequently over the city, which remains under a suffocating siege, with no medical supplies, water or fuel getting in,” al-Yamani reported.

“On the western front, there were intermittent clashes around dawn. The northern fronts were relatively calm, but still saw sporadic fighting. There has been a notable escalation in hostilities around Jabal Saber and Jabal Habashi,” he said.

articles.title: Pentagon asks Baltic Nato allies to tone down rhetoric on Russia threat: Report
articles.summary: Pentagon officials have privately urged several Nato allies in recent weeks to tone down their public comments on the threat from Russia, saying remarks
articles.body: Pentagon officials have privately urged several Nato allies in recent weeks to tone down their public comments on the threat from Russia, saying remarks by some European leaders could weaken security across the continent, news agency Reuters reported, citing four people familiar with the discussions.Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are among the countries that have received the message from Washington, the sources said. The conversations took place during bilateral meetings. It remains unclear whether the US has made similar requests to other European governments.The move comes as US President Donald Trump's administration renews its push to bring an end to the war in Ukraine through negotiations. Now in its fifth year, the conflict has become the focus of fresh diplomatic efforts by Washington, which has considered incentives for Moscow, including sanctions relief, while pressing Kyiv to stop attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.A Pentagon official declined to discuss the reported conversations, saying: "Private conversations among allies are just that, so we will not comment on these allegations."According to one of the people familiar with the discussions, US officials have taken issue with remarks by some European leaders portraying Russia as cornered and increasingly desperate as its advance in Ukraine slows.Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby, who is overseeing a key review of US troop deployments in Europe, was among those who conveyed the message, the sources said. Reuters could not establish who else from the US side was involved.The people, three European officials and one US official, said the exchanges were cordial and did not involve any confrontation.Pentagon's message: Avoid 'poking' RussiaThe reported US intervention highlights differences within Nato over how its members should speak publicly about Russia's growing assertiveness.Some Western officials believe strong warnings about Moscow's intentions could serve the Kremlin's interests by creating fear and weakening public support for Ukraine.Others argue that European governments need to openly communicate the Russian threat to their citizens. They say this is necessary to build support for the resources and sacrifices required to deter Moscow, particularly as concerns grow over an alleged Russian sabotage campaign across Europe. Russia has denied pursuing such a campaign.One person familiar with the matter told Reuters that Colby recently advised a Baltic official against "poking" the Russians.The official said Colby referred to comments suggesting Russia was "cornered like a rat", describing such language as unhelpful.It is not clear which specific remark he had in mind. However, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal had used the phrase "rat in a corner" for Russian President Vladimir Putin in late September. Michal had suggested that Moscow was turning to sabotage in Europe as its military campaign in Ukraine became increasingly bogged down.A separate European official described the tone of the Pentagon's private communication to Reuters, saying: "We are helping you. The Americans are there. Just don't be loud. Don't make noise."During another recent meeting, US officials asked an Estonian delegation to be "measured" in its public communication, a person briefed on the meeting said. The person did not specify whether the Pentagon had objected to any particular statement.The defence ministries of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia did not respond to requests for comment. Nato also declined to comment.European concerns grow over Russia's actionsOne European official said the Pentagon's advice was difficult to understand, despite the cordial manner in which it was delivered. The official noted that intelligence agencies in the Baltic states had repeatedly played down the chances of Russia testing Nato's collective defence commitments in recent months.Several other Nato intelligence services, however, have publicly warned that Moscow could step up its sabotage operations in the coming months.The discussions come amid growing concerns over covert attacks targeting Nato countries. Western intelligence officials say Russia has recently intensified such operations, although Moscow has denied involvement in a sabotage campaign.On Wednesday, German prosecutors announced the arrest of two Belarusians suspected of planning to set fire to a building or a critical infrastructure facility in the Nuremberg area.Earlier, in September, the German government accused Russia of being behind an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Moscow denied the allegations.Meanwhile, Washington has been exploring possible business agreements with Moscow as part of Trump's efforts to negotiate an end to the Ukraine war. The approach has not found unanimous support among European governments, many of which favour maintaining economic pressure on the Kremlin.The Pentagon is also reviewing the deployment of US forces across Europe. The exercise could lead to a substantial reduction in the American military presence on the continent.Washington has repeatedly called on European Nato members to take greater responsibility for their own defence. US officials have argued that America needs to focus more resources on security challenges in the Middle East, Latin America and East Asia.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.summary: British streamer Caedrel has climbed to the top of the Parasocial Streaming 100 rankings for the week of October 26, 2026.
articles.body: British streamer Caedrel has climbed to the top of the Parasocial Streaming 100 rankings for the week of October 26, 2026. His long streaming sessions during the League of Legends World Championship, also known as Worlds 2026, helped him reach the No. 1 spot. According to Parasocial Magazine, Caedrel recorded an estimated 6.4 million hours watched during the week. He also had an average of 146,879 viewers watching his streams at the same time, showing the huge interest in his Worlds broadcasts.Caedrel reaches No. 1 in streaming rankings after a strong Worlds 2026 runCaedrel moved up two places to claim the top spot in the latest Streaming 100 list. He was ranked No. 3 in the previous week's chart, but his strong performance during Worlds 2026 helped him move ahead of other creators.The figures were shared by Parasocial Magazine using data from Borealis, its creator tracking platform. The platform estimated that Caedrel's streams received 6.4 million hours of total watch time during the week. His average number of viewers was 146,879.The main reason behind this rise was his long run of co-streaming the League of Legends World Championship. Co-streaming means watching a live event and sharing it with viewers while giving personal comments and reactions.Caedrel is known for his League of Legends content, and Worlds gave his audience plenty of matches and moments to watch. His marathon broadcasts helped bring large numbers of viewers to his channel throughout the week.Worlds 2026 co-streams help Caedrel return to the top of the Streaming 100This is not the first time Caedrel has reached No. 1 on the Parasocial Streaming 100. He first appeared at the top of the chart on July 6, 2026. articles.title: US weighs new Iran strikes as Vance reaches out: Is war or a deal closer?
articles.summary: As Washington and Tehran send mixed signals, analysts say trust remains a key obstacle to any deal.
articles.body:
Over the past week, Washington and Tehran have sent mixed signals about whether their eight-month war is heading back to full-scale strikes or towards a peace deal.

On Thursday, the head of United States Central Command (CENTCOM), Admiral Brad Cooper, briefed US President Donald Trump on options for renewed attacks on Iran, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported.

The US and Israel have drawn up joint plans to attack Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections, The New York Times (NYT) reported last week.

Yet on the same day, The Washington Post reported that Vice President JD Vance had offered to meet Mohsen Rezaei , the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, in person to negotiate an end to the war.

On Friday, Qatari mediators returned to Tehran for talks coordinated with the US, an official told Reuters.

So is Washington heading back to war, or towards a deal? Here’s what we know:

Essentially, Washington is preparing for war while keeping a diplomatic channel open.

The WSJ reported that the US has boosted air defences and munitions in the region and moved some troops away from bases vulnerable to Iranian retaliation.

Ten US military cargo planes landed at the Ovda and Nevatim air bases in Israel’s Negev region on Thursday, with more sent to Jordan, Saudi Arabia and Qatar, the Israeli public broadcaster Kan reported.

Democratic Senator Chris Murphy, who said he had been briefed on the plans, called them “insane” and warned of a devastating escalation.

Can diplomatic efforts hold off a return to strikes?

Vance’s letter, delivered to Rezaei through Qatari mediators on Sunday, proposed direct talks led by Vance, with Iran’s nuclear programme on the table from the start, according to the NYT, in a bid to prevent a renewal of strikes.

Whether it might have any influence over what happens next is a matter for debate. Rouzbeh Parsi, an Iran analyst who is an affiliated researcher at Lund University’s Department of History and Human Rights Studies in Sweden, described Vance as the “voice of reason” on Iran within the Trump administration, saying his signals have been “the least volatile and unpredictable”.

But he also told Al Jazeera that Vance’s position has “never proven to be sturdy enough to actually sway Trump”.

“Thus, while the optics with Vance look better than anyone else in the Trump administration, I doubt that they [Iranian officials] give the outreach much credence until Vance proves able to actually deliver something on his own,” he said.

Furthermore, Nader Hashemi, a professor of Middle East politics at Georgetown University, told Al Jazeera that “Rezaei is just one voice among many” adding that the “reality is that decisions are made collectively inside the Islamic republic”.

Wolfgang Pusztai, a security and defence analyst and Austria’s former defence attache to Libya, has a different view, however, telling Al Jazeera, “There is no doubt that the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] currently calls the shots in Iran.”

In February, Iran’s then supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in the initial attacks by Israel and the United States, and his son became the new supreme leader, but Pusztai says he “simply does not have the influence his father did”.

“Without the IRGC’s approval, there will be no agreement with Iran,” Pusztai said, adding it is safe to assume that when Rezaei makes a statement or endorses a proposal, “it reflects the position of the IRGC leadership” and that the US was “absolutely right to negotiate with him”.

Pusztai said it is unclear whether Rezaei is indeed ready to make a serious compromise, but under sustained US pressure, Rezaei, who holds a doctorate in economics, could come to see that “Iran’s interests and the regime’s survival can be better secured without nuclear weapons and through a less aggressive foreign policy”.

“He certainly knows that peak oil is approaching and that time is running out for Iran’s economic recovery through the use of its oil revenues,” he said.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said progress depends on Iran’s seven conditions being met – including the lifting of sanctions, ending the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, guarantees to an end to US-Israeli strikes, and the unfreezing of Iranian assets – adding that the “carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran”, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

Vance, meanwhile, told Fox News on Thursday that Trump would “never” let the conflict become “a forever war”.

The diplomacy may say more than the threats.

Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of security studies at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that Vance’s offer of direct talks “suggests that the Americans do have second thoughts” and that they are less ready to strike than they publicly suggest.

But he warned that Cooper, whom he called “quite hawkish”, could give Trump false confidence “that there is a military way out of it, when in reality there isn’t a military way out of it”.

“This idea that there is a short and crisp military operation to solve this issue is obviously an illusion,” he said.

Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera the White House could be sending signals to coerce Tehran, but that “the better interpretation is the simplest one”.

He believes “the United States is getting ready to carry out substantial attacks relatively soon”. He said he does not expect Washington to accept what he called the unfavourable deal Tehran is offering “without another round of attacks”.

Pusztai said Trump’s main focus is now the midterms, making it “very unlikely that he will order another large-scale attack on Iran before the elections”.

“Starting in mid to late November, there could be a major wave of attacks aimed at advancing the American agenda,” he said, adding that the aim would be to weaken the IRGC enough to push it towards a deal on US terms.

Whatever the vote’s result, “in the short term it will not change much”, Musgrave said.

A strong Republican showing could encourage more aggressive tactics, while a Democratic win could push Trump to show his unilateral powers, including by attacking, he said.

It has. Iran was attacked by Israel or the US while talks were under way in both 2025 and 2026.

“We’ve seen this pattern of behaviour before from the United States,” Hashemi said, describing it as “talking diplomacy while preparing for war”.

On June 13, 2025, Israel launched major strikes on Iranian nuclear and military sites, two days before a sixth round of US-Iran talks was due in Oman. The US joined on June 22, bombing Iran’s Natanz, Fordow and Isfahan nuclear sites.

This year, the US and Israel attacked on February 28, two days after talks in Geneva that mediator Oman said had made “significant progress”.

A day before the strikes, Oman’s foreign minister said Iran had agreed to reduce its nuclear stockpiles to “the lowest level possible”.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera in September that Iran no longer trusts negotiations with Washington because attacks had come during previous rounds of talks.

Hashemi said he suspects “the same pattern is repeating itself”, with the US preparing “a massive bombing campaign in Iran, replete with war crimes like we haven’t seen before”, citing his reading of Murphy’s comments.

“The issue is mostly around sequencing and the lack of trust on the Iranian side that the Americans will actually follow through with their commitments,” Krieg said.

Tehran wants sanctions and the US naval blockade lifted quickly, fearing that a slow process gives Trump room to backtrack, he said.

Some IRGC hardliners do not necessarily see war as a bad thing if it tightens their grip on the Hormuz strait, he added, and “the Iranians have been prepping for this war for the last three weeks, so they are ready to fight”.

Krieg said he expects “nothing is going to happen until the 3rd of November [the date of the US midterm elections]”. After that, he said, the likelihood of war will “increase exponentially”.

Any new escalation would be worse than in February and March, he said, with Iran readier to strike critical infrastructure in Gulf countries.

He said the threat to the Gulf “will be unprecedented”.

articles.title: How can Israel break its election deadlock?
articles.summary: No political party has achieved the 61-seat majority required in the Knesset to form a government in Israel.
articles.body:
No clear winner has emerged from Israel’s election , raising speculation over which party could form the next government.

Early on Friday, the Central Elections Committee (CEC) published the final results of the October 27 vote, which had a high voter turnout of 77.9 percent.

Neither Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor the opposition grouping led by Gadi Eisenkot has secured the majority necessary to form a government. Both leaders have also ruled out working with the two main electoral lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List.

So how can Israel break its political deadlock?

Yes. On Thursday, at least 500,000 “double envelope” votes which came in from soldiers and diplomats were counted. These voters use two envelopes: the first contains their ballot without any identifying information, while the second bears their personal details. The anonymous envelope is placed inside the second envelope, allowing officials to check that voters have not cast ballots elsewhere, without compromising the secrecy of their choice.

Netanyahu’s bloc secured 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot won 48 seats.

The United Arab List, or Ra’am, and the Joint List secured a combined 19 seats.

To form a government, a political party must hold at least 61 seats. No single party has ever won that majority and alliances have led to governing coalitions, with a prime minister at the helm.

Political consultations to form a coalition are reported to be under way.

If the process fails, Israeli President Isaac Herzog could choose which candidate has the best chance to form a government. That candidate is then given about 28 days to do so – a period that could be extended.

If the candidate fails, the president can then choose another. If that candidate is unable to form a government, then a 21-day window opens in which 61 members of the Knesset can submit a request to Herzog to assign the task to a Knesset member.

Yes, because if all the processes listed above fail, Israelis will have to return to the polls.

Are Arab parties being considered for coalitions?

Many Israeli leaders have rejected the idea of partnering with Arab-led parties .

Netanyahu has ruled out working alongside them and demonised them following their strong showing.

“It is forbidden to form a government with them,” Netanyahu posted on X on Friday.

Netanyahu’s Likud party has accused the Arab-led parties of “stealing” the election, after his own coalition lost its majority.

According to a Times of Israel report this week, Eisenkot has said he would only consider partnering with any party that recognises Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, endorses the values of the Declaration of Independence and commits to all Israelis performing national service.

He has not said whether the Arab-led parties would meet those criteria.

On Thursday, another opposition figure, Avigdor Lieberman, the hard-right leader of Yisrael Beytenu, also ruled out certain coalitions. “Neither Bibi nor Tibi”, he said, using Netanyahu’s nickname and invoking Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Ta’al party – part of the Joint List.

The Arab parties have shown interest in partnering with anti-Netanyahu factions.

Yousef Jabareen from the Joint List said that his party was ready for the “ousting of the Netanyahu government”, which he called one of “bloodshed”.

“Against a politics of supremacy, racism, and exclusion, we offer a completely different alternative. The change comes through Jewish-Arab partnership, a true and equal partnership,” he wrote on X.

Political analyst Ahmed Najar said the parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel have shown considerably more pragmatism than Eisenkot and most of his allies.

“Ra’am has indicated that it is open to participating in an Eisenkot-led government, while the Joint List has left open the possibility of supporting a minority government from outside the coalition, provided that such support delivers meaningful commitments on equality, violent crime in Palestinian communities, home demolitions and a political pathway for the wider Palestinian question,” he said.

Can Arab parties break the political deadlock?

It is still too soon to say, according to analysts.

“The numbers don’t add up for any side,” Roi Zur, a lecturer at Essex University and specialist in Israeli voting behaviour and election strategies, told Al Jazeera. “However, there are rumours that Eisenkot will ask for the support of the Arab parties in a government investiture vote in return for financial investment in their communities. Yet, this is unlikely on both sides, and even if both sides go forward with this idea, it might fall due to Lieberman objecting to the idea.”

Zur said that if the four parties in Eisenkot’s “change bloc” were closer to a majority, outside support would have been more likely because Ra’am is perceived as a more “moderate” Arab party.

“Then a European-style confidence-and-supply agreement would be more probable,” he added.

Nimrod Flaschenberg, a Berlin-based political analyst, told Al Jazeera that it is still unclear whether Eisenkot is willing to rely on Ra‘am and the Joint List.

“If Eisenkot will be willing to go for such cooperation, then there are three options: The first is the Israeli-Arab parties could be part of the government. This is what Ra‘am wants; the Joint List does not want this at this stage. The second option is they could be a coalition member but without any government seats. This is what Ra‘am was in the Bennet government from 2021-2022,” he said.

“The third option is they could support from the outside as a preventive bloc that does not vote down the government. Most predict that if there is such a government, it will include Ra‘am in the coalition and will rely on the Joint List from the outside,” he added.

Palestinian political analyst Najar said that the real obstacle at this stage is not a lack of pragmatism from Arab parties, but rather “the refusal of Eisenkot and several of his partners to recognise Palestinian citizens of Israel – and the 19 representatives they elected – as legitimate political partners”.

“The election produced 67 seats outside Netanyahu’s bloc, but Israel’s political system continues to behave as though 19 of those seats do not fully count. Eisenkot wants Palestinian votes to remove Netanyahu while insisting on a ‘Zionist government’ that excludes the representatives of those same voters,” he noted.

“That is not merely coalition arithmetic; it exposes a profound democratic contradiction. Palestinian citizens are permitted to vote, but when their votes become decisive, their political legitimacy is immediately questioned,” he added.

To keep power, the prime minister could yet form a coalition, according to Yossi Mekelberg, a senior consulting fellow with the Middle East and North Africa Programme at Chatham House.

“He can try and persuade Eisenkot and others to form a coalition with him and in the meantime he can delegitimise the Arab parties to make it difficult to form an alternative government,” he told Al Jazeera.

Flaschenberg said Netanyahu will likely push for another round of elections.

“In his calculation – the Arabs will not turn out as before and the opposition would be discouraged and stagnant. He believes that in another round of elections his bloc could get to 61,” he said.

“The other option that [Netanyahu] is working on is getting one or two parties from the Change bloc to join his government. Most likely Bennet and Liberman. But at the moment it doesn’t look like they are going to join him,” he added.

Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, called the election “an existential moment for Palestinian Israelis”.

Palestinian analyst Najar said that for Palestinian citizens of Israel, the result represents both an achievement and a test.

“They turned out in large numbers, secured unprecedented representation and may now have the power to prevent another Netanyahu government. Yet they are again being told that their votes are acceptable only if they do not translate into real political power,” he said.

“For Palestinians in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, however, there is little reason to see this as a contest between occupation and peace, or between oppression and equality. It is principally a struggle over who will govern Israel and how Israel will present itself — not whether Palestinians will continue to live under military occupation, settlement expansion, dispossession and systemic inequality,” he added.

“But Palestinians will judge any successor by policy, not personality – whether it ends the genocide in Gaza, stops settlement expansion and settler violence, and recognises Palestinian freedom and self-determination,” he said.

articles.title: They said he couldn’t travel due to his disability. Today, he’s visited all seven continents
articles.summary: With his mom by his side, Cory Lee has explored 56 countries by wheelchair. Now he’s helping others discover how far they can go.
articles.body: At 36, Cory Lee has a travel record few can match: 56 countries and all seven continents (yes, even Antartica). Remarkably, he’s accomplished this feat while using a 400-pound power wheelchair — navigating not just the globe but formidable accessibility barriers. “I cannot physically use the restroom on a plane, so I’m usually dehydrating and starving myself for a couple days before the flight,” Cory told CNN. “On the day of the flight, I have to physically be lifted out of my wheelchair and put onto the plane and into my seat. On several occasions I’ve been dropped. “I’m constantly worried if my power wheelchair is going to be damaged in the cargo hold because frequently it’s not tied down,” he added. “That happens all the time — I arrived in Barcelona a couple years ago and the front wheel caster was snapped in half. In Atlanta, the joystick was missing, and I couldn’t leave the airport.” The effort it takes for Cory to travel is “insane, so much more than I have to do,” said Cory’s friend Kelly Narowski, a disability rights advocate who uses a manual wheelchair after losing the use of her legs in a car accident. “His level of grit and perseverance is inspiring to me and many others, and I do not use the word ‘inspiring’ lightly,” said Kelly, who has traveled with Cory to Chile, Spain, Greece, Mexico, the Dominican Republic and the Bahamas. Cory shares his adventures and provides accessibility advice on his popular travel blog, “Curb Free with Cory Lee,” which reaches an international audience of wheelchair users and their caregivers who are searching for ways to enrich their lives. “Someone recognized him in a small town in Chile and again in Spain,” Kelly said. “He teaches young people with disabilities that they can still travel. It just is so heartwarming — he really changes lives.” ‘The wheelchair is their freedom’ Cory’s been on so many adventures since he started his blog in 2013 that it’s hard for him to choose his favorites. A safari in Africa stands out: “I was able to touch a hippo — the whole trip really was such an incredible experience.” Thailand, said Cory, “blew my mind — I was able to feed elephants and get a tattoo from a monk at a monastery in Thailand, which was really something! “I’ve gone paragliding in the Swiss Alps. I’ve gone ziplining. I’ve gone snow skiing,” he said. “Travel really pushes me to break out of my comfort zone and embrace the world.” Arriving in Antarctica, Cory recalled crying. “It was such an emotional moment for me, because I had worked so long and so hard to get to that point,” he said to CNN in a 2020 profile. One of his most unusual experiences was a camel ride in 2018 in Morocco – the first of many annual “Curb Free” group tours that Cory organizes for wheelchair users. “A company in Morocco actually invented the world’s first adapted camel saddle,” he said. “I will never forget being on that camel and looking out at the dunes of the Sahara Desert, pinching myself and thinking, ‘Is this even real?’ I never knew that I could have an experience like that as a wheelchair user.” Cory’s mom, 57-year-old Sandy Gilbreath, is his constant travel partner, wrangling most everything — luggage, wheelchair repair, bathrooms, meals, showers and bedtime. “He’s changed my life completely and my outlook on others with disabilities,” Sandy told CNN. “Someone in a wheelchair — I now see them as a person first. “The wheelchair is not what disables them — the wheelchair is their freedom. It’s their independence,” she added. “It’s society and the limitations that are in the world for people with disabilities that is the problem.” ‘You’re an overprotective mom’ When 1-year-old Cory’s knees buckled as he tried to walk, Sandy knew something was terribly wrong. “His legs would just give out, and his head would actually smack the floor before I could rush over and stop him,” she said. “I had taken him to pediatricians and tried to find out, ‘Is this normal? What’s going on?’ They kept saying, ‘Oh, you’re an overprotective mom.’ Finally, at that 2-year mark, I was like, ‘We’ve got to do something,’ and so they did a muscle biopsy on him.” Cory was diagnosed with spinal muscular atrophy type 2, or SMA, a progressive genetic disorder caused by the loss of motor neurons in the spinal cord. After cystic fibrosis, SMA is the second most common severe hereditary disease in childhood. As the disease progresses, muscles deteriorate, limiting the ability to hold one’s head upright, sit without support, raise arms or even breathe. Traditionally, some 70% of people with SMA live to the age of 25; some make it into their 30s. “It was devastating, absolutely devastating,” Sandy said. “I called my parents, and I was like, ‘He’s got a muscle-wasting disease that there’s no cure for, and it’s just going to get worse over time.’ “My dad answered the phone that day, and he’s always been my rock, my go-to,” she said. “He never even skipped a beat. He said, ‘There’s a lot of things that people have wrong with them, but it’s how you deal with those challenges that make the difference.’ From that day on, I thought, ‘This is it. This is life. We’re going to make the best of it, and we move forward from there.’” The disease progressed quickly. By age 4, Cory relied on a power wheelchair that required an accessible van. Sandy, now a single mom, had no money for a proper ramp or the equipment that could make caring for him easier. “When I say we were poor, I’m not even kidding,” she said. “I struggled to buy groceries, to have gas to take him to therapy — swimming therapy, because in the water he was weightless, so he could move his arms, move his legs. It was 45 minutes from our house, and we had to go three days a week, and I didn’t have the gas money to take him.” ‘If you can’t stand up, stand out’ Despite the family’s challenges, Cory thrived. Carolyn Huggins, his daily caregiver throughout elementary and high school in his small, rural town in Georgia, remembers Cory as an extremely smart child who was “very sensitive to people’s feelings.” “The young ladies at school, they just loved Cory,” Carolyn said. “They always wanted to help him during the school day — carry his book bag, his lunch tray, whatever. I think it was because Cory was such a sweet young man, and he just loved people.” Cory pursued every opportunity that came his way. He was student council vice president twice and a member of the German Club, Beta Club and Drama Club. He also performed outside of school, starring in several plays across northwest Georgia. “I jokingly tell people I’ve always felt like Cory didn’t even know he was disabled,” Sandy said. “Mentally, yes, he knows his limitations, but he never acted like he was disabled. He wanted to be in the spotlight, never shy or embarrassed or hiding his wheelchair. I don’t know where it came from, but I’m glad he had it.” Cory credits his family, and especially his mom, for his positive attitude toward life. “My mom, when I was growing up, she always told me: ‘If you can’t stand up, stand out.’ That’s been a motto I’ve lived with,” Cory said. “I’ve also not really known life outside of a wheelchair, so I don’t necessarily see myself as disabled. “Society sees me that way, but I don’t see me that way. I was just taught to always stand out and rise above any situation that society wants to throw on me.” The rejection that changed everything As he headed towards graduation with a bachelor’s degree in marketing, Cory started job hunting, with little luck. Then a breakthrough: An advertising firm wanted him to fly to Pennsylvania for an interview. “I was super excited. I flew to Pittsburgh the next day,” Cory said. “As soon as I rolled into the hiring manager’s office, he looked me up and down and I could sense he really only saw the wheelchair and didn’t see me as a person.” Before the interview began, it was over. “It wasn’t even five minutes,” said Sandy, who was waiting in the lobby. “Cory was right back out, tears rolling down his face. He told me the hiring manager looked at him and said, ‘This job is going to require a lot of travel, and you’re definitely not the best fit for this.’ And then the man walked back out of the room. “Now, it’s unbelievable that Cory’s career is travel. But flying home from that job interview, we’re crying on the plane and I’m thinking, ‘What is his life going to be like? What will he do now? Nobody’s seeing past the chair.” Ironically, before the interview Cory had been dreaming of a graduation trip to Australia. His internet searches for accessible travel information came up short, exposing yet another obstacle for people with disabilities. “I thought, I’ll launch an accessible travel blog as a hobby — I never expected it to take over my life in the way that it has. Yet, it’s been the best thing that could have ever happened to me,” Cory said. “I can finally communicate with other people that actually understand what it’s like to live and travel with a disability. It’s been the best experience in the world.” A booming business As Cory’s online audience grew, he was invited to give speeches and attend business conferences on accessible travel, broadening his reach. “Travel destinations started reaching out to him and saying, ‘If you’ll come here and show what we’re offering, we’ll pay for it. We’ll pay you.’ It’s just grown into something unbelievable for me and for Cory,” Sandy said. As the company blossomed, Sandy was able to quit her job as a Medicaid specialist and become a full-time employee, documenting their travels with videos and photographs and assisting with social media. She also co-authors children’s books with Cory and serves on the board of The Curb Free Foundation, a nonprofit they launched in 2022 to provide travel grants to wheelchair users. “They offered me the opportunity to make a dream a reality,” said Maylan Chavez, a Florida-based Francophile who won a grant to visit Paris after years of French lessons. “When I was at the opera and the Louvre, I would just cry a little bit, and say, ‘Wow, I can’t believe I’m here! I can’t believe I made it!’” said Maylan, who also has spinal muscular atrophy type 2. “Many of us with SMA, we can’t even do a three-hour road trip because we don’t have the means, or we don’t have an accessible car or caregivers to take us,” she said. “I know a lot of us are homebound, so being able to see Cory go to Indonesia and all over the world and then being able to do a trip myself was incredible.” As his health has worsened in recent years, Cory has been determined to visit as many places as possible before travel becomes too difficult. He and his mom took 24 trips over six months in 2025 and, so far in 2026, have taken 17 trips over four months. Next year’s plans include Beijing, Hong Kong and four group trips to Italy, with more to come. Sandy worries about her health as well. Despite doing daily core exercises for years — 200 crunches before bed and 50 squats while brushing her teeth in the morning — she fears the physical strain of lifting Cory in and out of planes, taxis, trains and trams could take a toll. “I’m not only stressed about his health and his equipment getting damaged, but I’m also worried about me. What if I got sick and we’re on a trip? Who’s going to help him?” she said. “I try to be positive, I really do. I’m always looking at the glass half full. But on the inside, it hurts to see your child struggle just to raise his arms to eat. I see those declines happening,” Sandy said. “But I just live for today. We’re going to do it as long as I’m able and as long as he’s willing to let me.” For Cory, too, the desire to keep traveling outweighs the difficulties. Travel makes him feel alive — and he hopes to spend years doing what he loves while challenging society’s narrow expectations of people with disabilities. “I have the best job in the world,” Cory said. “I hope my legacy shows able-bodied people just what people with disabilities are capable of, and that we can do so much and have so many incredible experiences. The more information and visibility we can get out into the world, the better.”

articles.title: DOUGLAS MACKINNON: This land is your land. This land is my land. But it’s not a DEI land
articles.summary: DEI and identity politics threaten meritocracy across the United States as commercial aviation, debanking and infrastructure safety face growing risks.
articles.body: Recently, I was on an extended business trip across the United States that ultimately touched upon planes, trains, automobiles, ships, bridges and majestic skyscrapers. Along the way, I honestly paused in awe to marvel at modern jetliners; the engines pulling passenger and freight trains cross-country; driverless taxis; four-football-field-long megacruise ships; the George Washington and the Golden Gate bridges; and 60-story-plus office towers in New York City, San Francisco and Los Angeles. As I pondered them all over the course of the trip, I had two immediate thoughts. The first being that, in one way or another, those modes of transportation and that stunning and often historic infrastructure all held human life within and upon them. The second was that all were devised and built via meritocracy. DEI, identity politics and woke dictates played no role in their construction. Nor should they ever, when what is being designed and built will eventually determine the safety of human lives. MEDICAL SCHOOLS ACCUSED OF REBRANDING DEI PROGRAMS TO EVADE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SCRUTINY My third and overriding thought was: "That’s all about to be thrown out the window once the ‘religion’ of wokeism comes roaring back into play across the spectrum of our lives." If you think otherwise, I most humbly believe you either have not been paying attention to current events or are fooling yourself via the cliché: "Ignorance is bliss." To be clear, I don’t care if someone is female, male, Black, White, brown, straight, gay, trans, liberal, conservative, faith-based or an atheist. articles.title: JACKSON THOMPSON: Gronk calls on NFL to punish refs, says Patriots made last Super Bowl due to easy schedule
articles.summary: Rob Gronkowski calls for NFL referee punishments, questions the Patriots' Super Bowl chances, and reveals Bill Belichick's strangest team rules.
articles.body: Rob Gronkowski is calling for the NFL to institute referee punishments amid a slew of questionable officiating decisions this season. The New England Patriots legend also revealed he is skeptical of his long-time team's chances at getting back to the Super Bowl, and suggested they made it last year due to a weak schedule. Gronkowki shared his bevy of strong takes, revealed some newly-unearthed secrets about Bill Belichick's strangest rules, and revealed a new technology he is using to heal his body from the wear and tear of football in an interview with OutKick. 'Put the referees on a pedestal' Gronkowski believes officials should face consequences just as the players and coaches whose games they help decide do. "So yeah, I think, you know, it would be fair and square to, you know, put the referees on a pedestal as well and — and have punishment just like any coach or any NFL player can be punished just like that," Gronkowski said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE Asked whether the NFL needs more accountability for officials, Gronkowski pointed to how quickly a player’s fortunes can change. "I think so, actually, because players are accountable. Players can be cut the very next day and you’ve seen players cut," he continued. Gronkowski’s comments followed Tom Brady’s criticism of several calls during the Detroit Lions’ 20-17 win over the Green Bay Packers during Sunday's NFL on FOX broadcast. Brady and FOX rules analyst Dean Blandino disputed multiple decisions, including roughing-the-passer penalties and an intentional grounding call. Gronkowski agreed with his former quarterback’s broader concerns. "I don’t think the referees are doing that great of a job. I think they can definitely improve," he said. He identified pass interference and roughing-the-passer calls as areas that need improvement before the postseason, warning that incorrect flags could determine games. "We want it to be fair and square. That’s what fans want to see," he said. "Yes, you call it when it’s appropriate, but when it’s not appropriate, you know, it doesn’t need to be called and affects the game in all ways." NFL FINES THREE HEAD COACHES $250,000 FOR THEIR CONDUCT TOWARD OFFICIALS: REPORT The NFL already grades officials on every play, according to its Football Operations website. Those evaluations help determine postseason assignments. Gronkowski also recalled his own frustration with offensive pass interference penalties when defenders collided with him. "It was just me running and I was just a bigger body. So the guy would bounce off of me, you know, even though he ran into me and then I would get the flag. It just didn’t make any sense," he said. Patriots have work to do before another Super Bowl run The Patriots enter Week 8 at 4-3 after a 30-24 loss to the Chicago Bears, and have shown signs of regression after reaching the Super Bowl last year. "Their schedule definitely was pretty, pretty simple last year. They’re playing tougher opponents this year, tougher defenses. I think that has more to play with it," Gronkowski said of the Patriots. "I definitely think the schedule plays a part in it for sure. It really does." Gronkowski sees a playoff team in New England. He is less convinced he sees a championship team. "The Patriots, I think, are a pretty solid, you know, football team. And I think they’re going to make the playoffs. They definitely have a chance at winning their division. They just got to pick it up," he said. "I just don’t see enough right now for them to be a potential, you know, Super Bowl candidate." NFL REFS HAVE SET ALL-TIME RECORD FOR FLAGS THIS SEASON, AND IT'S CHANGING THE OUTCOME OF GAMES Gronkowski also pointed offensive injuries and the need for more playmakers. He said New England’s offense had been clicking more consistently last season. "They’re just having some problems right now, a couple injuries, injuries all across the offensive line. They’re depleted there. So I think the injuries, you know, to the offensive unit is playing a crucial part as well," he said. "And once they get everyone back and AJ Brown gets fully healthy, I think they can start clicking at a high level then." Asked what he would bring to the current locker room, Gronkowski emphasized experience and a belief that the team can win regardless of the circumstances. "I would say just a mentality of bringing it at practice and also having just a winning mentality that, hey, no matter the situation, we’re going to come, we’re going to find a way to win this game," he said. Gronkowski’s health after football, and what Brady and Belichick taught him for life Gronkowski’s memories of the Patriots include Bill Belichick’s rules for what players could do away from the field — including a ban on burning incense in hotel rooms. "He said, not even incense are allowed to be burned in your hotel room," Gronkowski recalled, explaining that Belichick wanted to leave no room for interpretation about burning anything. But the rule that bothered him most involved where veteran players had to sleep during training camp. "I would just say the most wildest one, though, was having veteran players stay at the hotel, even though their homes are closer to the facility than the hotel throughout training camp," he said. "That definitely drove a couple of veteran players like myself crazy." Still, Gronkowski said he understood the reasoning behind Belichick’s strict approach. He credited Belichick and Brady with shaping his habits, calling them "the two biggest leaders of my life." Brady’s approach to food and preparation, in particular, offered a lesson Gronkowski could carry beyond football. "He didn’t force it down anyone, but you just watch him. That’s what it’s all about is leading by example," Gronkowski said. Now, Gronkowski’s own priorities include staying active and managing the physical toll of his playing career. "If you have your health, you know, you have everything," he said. He continues to work out and incorporates hot yoga, saunas and float tanks into his routine. He also discussed his partnership with DNA Vibe, whose Jazz Band wearable he credits with helping him manage aches and pains. "You got to ask someone that truly knows the science behind red light therapy, but, you know, I just like to do it because I’ve tried it, you know, through my own experiences and it works," he said. DNA Vibe founder and CEO Perry Kamel said the device combines red and infrared light, micro-vibration and magnetic pulses, which the company markets as supporting the body’s natural recovery processes. Both quarterbacks played in big games for Michigan, and then didn't have the smoothest starts to their NFL careers. McCarthy, the No. 10 overall pick in 2024, had to work his way back into a starting role after losing his job in Minnesota and getting traded to the Giants. Asked whether the focus on celebrity couples could annoy fans, Gronkowski rejected the idea that broadcasts have gone too far. articles.body: Trump calls on the DOJ to ramp up its investigations into Alaska’s Senate race. Israel’s final election results show no clear winner between Netanyahu and his main rival Eisenkot. And the cruise company that stranded its passengers in Cambodia has a troubled history. Here’s what to know today. Trump pushes to ramp up investigations into Alaska Senate race The Justice Department has issued at least three dozen new subpoenas and document preservation requests as part of its investigation into the Alaska Senate race, with President Donald Trump pushing his administration to intensify its investigations. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The action comes after the New York Times reported that Democratic candidate Mary Peltola’s campaign was involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan, a retired teacher with no previous political experience, to also run for the seat held by Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The neck-and-neck race, along with a handful of others, will decide whether Republicans retain control of the Senate. The subpoenas were sent to Peltola’s Senate campaign offices and those of Dan J. Sullivan. Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy also announced yesterday that he’s ordering an investigation into Peltola’s campaign, which denies involvement in the recruitment effort. The DOJ had opened a criminal investigation into the race in July. The new reporting now gives the president more ammunition for the probe, which revolves around potential violations of federal laws that protect citizens’ rights to free and fair elections. Trump also ordered the department to file a civil lawsuit to try to block the state from certifying election results. What legal experts say about asking someone to run for office. Pope Leo could become the first pontiff to vote in a U.S. election after requesting an Illinois absentee ballot. Former FBI Director James Comey is expected in court today as he seeks to toss out the third criminal case the Trump administration has brought against him. Israel’s final election results show no clear leader Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing bloc won 53 seats in Israel’s 120-member Knesset, or parliament, well below the 68 seats it had controlled at its peak in the previous parliament. The bloc supporting Netanyahu’s main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats. Neither secured the 61 seats needed to form a government. While the count is complete, the election results still need to be certified and submitted to Israeli President Isaac Herzog, who will then choose a candidate who he thinks has the best chance to form a government. What else to know about the election results. Parties led by Israel’s Arab minority, meanwhile, made historic gains, winning a combined 19 seats in the Knesset, after Palestinians with Israeli citizenship headed to the polls in record numbers. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot’s blocs have ruled out the possibility of forming a government with the two main Arab parties. Yet the political parties’ rise as potential kingmakers has brought a complicated dynamic into fresh focus. Patrick Stewart, ‘Star Trek’ and ‘X-Men’ actor, dies at 86 Tributes have poured in for Patrick Stewart, the beloved English actor who rose from performing Shakespeare on stage to becoming a globally-recognized movie icon. Stewart died this week at age 86 after a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia, his representative said. His storied career included cultural high points as Capt. Jean-Luc Picard in the “Star Trek” franchise and as Professor Charles Xavier in the “X-Men” films. Actor Ian McKellen said in a tribute that his dear friend “wore his heart on his sleeve, which made him a man to rely on, to admire and in my case, love.” Though the two met in the 1970s, their bond was solidified when they starred together in “X-Men.” Read more about their decadeslong friendship. Kevin Feige, president of Marvel Studios, recalled being “in awe” of Stewart the first time he saw him on the set of the first X-Men, describing him as “brilliant, charming, warm, generous, with a quiet strength and gravitas.” The Royal Shakespeare Company hailed Stewart as “one of the finest classical Shakespearean actors of his generation.” Read more about Stewart’s life and legacy. Binance targeted in largest ever crypto heist The digital currency exchange Binance said it was the target of a $6.3 billion crypto heist, believed to be the largest ever recorded. The company has suspended all deposits and withdrawals while it works with law enforcement to secure its infrastructure and locate stolen funds. About $3 billion of crytpo assets that transited through wallets connected to the hackers have so far been identified and frozen, the company said. Binance said it will “cover all the losses,” but cautioned that the value of the affected assets, as well as those recovered or frozen, could change. Earlier Thursday, prediction markets platform Polymarket briefly halted trading because of a compromise of third-party software. There were also some unconfirmed reports from users that their wallets had been drained. Here’s what else we know about the heist. Staff Pick: Cruise company had legal troubles before abandoning passengers Villa Vie, the cruise company that promised sailors a life-long worldwide voyage, boasts a troubled company history in its short existence. Since its creation in 2023, Villa Vie has been plagued by several lawsuits alleging breaches of contract, sudden itinerary changes and delays, and failure to pay employees earned overtime. It also failed a health inspection and its owners have both faced bankruptcy. More than 200 passengers, some of whom sold their homes to live aboard, are stranded in Cambodia with nowhere to go and no promise of reimbursement after the company said high fuel prices halted the cruise. One woman who sued Villa Vie, Jenny Phenix, said she was kicked off the cruise before it even started after she expressed concerns in what she thought was a private WhatsApp group chat. The messages, she said, got back to management. “There were numerous things to complain about,” she told NBC News. “Between the delays, the lack of notice for the delays, what we were paying out of pocket and all of the, you know, just watching all of the amenities you expected just disappearing before your eyes to where now this is not a luxury cruise anymore. It’s nothing like what you signed up for.” — Rebecca Cohen, reporter Read All About It New audio reveals the moments before a deadly train crash in Spain, including an operator saying she could not restart her stopped train before the collision. articles.title: Russia ‘forces’ closure of investigative newspaper Novaya Gazeta
articles.summary: A symbol of independent journalism, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a ‘foreign agent’ by Moscow.
articles.body:
Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta has announced it will shut down, citing pressure from the authorities.

The independent outlet’s editorial board said in a statement released on Friday that the newspaper has been forced to end its operations.

The Russian media has come under increased scrutiny from the state amid Moscow’s war on Ukraine. The authorities recently searched the home of Novaya Gazeta’s senior editor and arrested the editor-in-chief.

“The newspaper is gone. The Russian authorities and … intelligence services forced the editorial staff to cease operations,” the editorial board said in the statement , which was entitled: “We were killed.”

Viewed as a relative bastion of independent journalism in Russia, Novaya Gazeta has been classed as a “foreign agent” by Moscow, a label used to stifle dissent.

“Novaya Gazeta is ceasing to exist,” editor-in-chief Sergei Sokolov said in a video statement published on YouTube. “On November 9 we will turn off the lights in our home, where we have lived for 30 years. We will shut down the servers and leave.”

Earlier this month, Sokolov was taken in for questioning as Russian authorities searched his home due, they said, to a link to a criminal case involving his colleague Oleg Roldugin.

Roldugin was arrested in April and charged with “unlawful access to computerised information”.

“How far will the Kremlin’s relentless campaign against Novaya Gazeta go?” asked media watchdog Reporters Without Borders in a statement after Sokolov was arrested on October 15.

“Six of its journalists and staff members have been murdered, its newsroom has been raided, its journalists have been prosecuted, and the publication has been designated a ‘foreign agent’,” the press freedom organisation noted.

The forced closure of Novaya Gazeta marks another escalation in Russia’s crackdown on press freedom, with few independent media outlets or journalists left in the country, as censorship levels and arrests of regime critics have skyrocketed since it launched its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The newspaper had already trimmed production inside Russia after Moscow invaded Ukraine, as authorities revoked its media licence.

The paper’s then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Muratov, jointly won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021 for his “efforts to safeguard freedom of expression” at the helm of the paper.

articles.title: Tributes pour in for Bristol-trained actor Sir Patrick Stewart
articles.summary: Tributes are paid to the Bristol Old Vic Theatre-trained star of stage and screen, after his death at 86.
articles.body:
Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, has been described as a "treasured" actor and a "true champion" of the Bristol theatre school he trained at.

Tributes have poured in since Sir Patrick's death at his Los Angeles home on Wednesday after a "brief and poignant journey" with Alzheimer's disease and Lewy Body Dementia, according to a statement shared on his social media.

The acclaimed actor, who found global fame in Shakespeare productions, Star Trek and X-Men, had trained at the Bristol Old Vic Theatre School from the age of 17.

He was also a patron of local theatre company Unique Voice which tours schools, running drama workshops to educate children about domestic violence.

A spokesperson for the charity said: "He knew he stood upon a stage and he used that stage on behalf of others countless times."

Bristol then and now: Trams, barges and rugby

Hope for stranded canal boats with tunnel repair plan

The man who chooses to sleep with bedbugs

In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.

His most notable roles included Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men films.

He also had a distinguished stage career with the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) that established him as one of the country's leading Shakespearean actors.

Bristol Old Vic Theatre School (BOVTS) principal Stuart Harvey said his "exceptional" career stood as a testament to "the power of rigorous classical training".

He said: "Before becoming an international icon on stage and screen, Patrick honed his craft right here at the school as a member of the class of 1959.

"In recent years, we were deeply privileged to receive Sir Patrick's support. He remained forever proud of his BOVTS heritage.

"His legacy as a master of his craft and a true champion of our school will endure always."

Fellow alumnus and theatre director Sir Gregory Doran worked alongside Sir Stewart on a production of Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra in 2006.

He recalled how the acclaimed actor "restored the magnificence" of the role.

"I'm realising that was why he was so great - he had this very solid, firm foundation [of training]," he said.

"That allowed him, in a way, to take the helm of the Starship Enterprise and fly around the galaxies. I shall miss him greatly."

Sir Doran said a performance of Romeo and Juliet at the Tobacco Factory in Bristol later would be dedicated to his memory.

Outside of work, Sir Patrick was a prominent campaigner against domestic abuse after witnessing his father beating his mother as a child.

He became a voluntary patron for Unique Voice in 2011, with co-director Krystal Keeley describing him as a "perfect fit" and an "amazing inspiration".

She said: "When we met him we were still like 'we can't believe you've chosen us', but he said it was a no-brainer.

"He cared deeply about giving a voice to people who were underserved. We will be forever grateful to him and incredibly proud that he chose to stand alongside us.

"He did it all with such warmth, such genuine care and kindness. It's a very sad day that the world has lost such a treasured artist."
