articles.title: Psychology says people who remember a particular hug years later may be recalling the feeling of comfort more than the gesture itself; a new study of over 15,000 adults finds why some embraces stay with us
articles.summary: Think about a hug you still remember, even though it happened years ago.
articles.body: Think about a hug you still remember, even though it happened years ago. It may have come from a parent when you were upset, a friend who knew you were struggling, or someone you had not seen in a long time. You may not remember exactly where you were standing or how long the embrace lasted. But you remember how you felt afterwards.A new study suggests that this emotional response may be what makes certain hugs stay in our memories. Researchers from the University of Bristol and other institutions found that people were more likely to remember a hug because it made them feel comforted, supported or understood than because of the physical gesture itself.The research, published in the journal PLOS One, analysed responses from 15,049 adults in the UK. It examined whether people remembered a hug for its positive emotional impact and whether personality and individual differences were associated with these memories. Nearly seven in 10 participants, 69.5% said they could recall a hug that had a positive emotional effect on them.What makes a hug memorable?The researchers found that comfort was the most commonly selected reason for remembering a hug. Other reasons included feeling supported, understood, happy or connected to someone. This suggests that a hug can become meaningful because of what it communicates at a particular moment. When someone embraces us during a difficult period, the gesture may convey reassurance without requiring an explanation. A hug after a long separation may communicate affection, while one offered during grief may make a person feel that they are not facing the situation alone.The researchers also examined whether individual characteristics could help explain why some people remembered these experiences more strongly than others. People who scored higher on measures of empathy and awareness of their bodily experiences were more likely to recall an emotionally meaningful hug. Those who were less comfortable with emotional closeness, measured through attachment-related avoidance, were less likely to report such memories.The study also found differences between men and women in the reasons they remembered particular hugs. Women were more likely to identify comfort as the reason, while men were more likely to report physical arousal, friendliness or understanding. These differences were relatively small and should not be treated as fixed rules about how men and women experience affection.Why do some people remember these moments more strongly?The findings suggest that memories of physical affection are not shaped by touch alone. The relationship between the people involved, the emotional situation and an individual's comfort with closeness may all influence how the experience is remembered.For instance, a hug from someone who has been emotionally supportive may carry a different meaning from an otherwise similar hug from an acquaintance. The physical action may look the same, but the personal significance can be very different.The researchers also considered attachment styles, which describe patterns in how people experience closeness and relationships. People with higher attachment-related avoidance may be less comfortable depending on others or expressing emotional closeness. This could partly explain why they were less likely to recall a hug for its positive emotional impact.However, the study does not establish that attachment style causes people to remember or forget particular hugs. It identifies associations between reported characteristics and memories.What the research cannot tell usThe study offers an interesting look at how adults remember affectionate touch, but it has limitations. Participants were asked to recall their own experiences, so the findings depend on personal memory and self-reported responses.The sample was also drawn from the UK, and women made up around 75% of participants. The researchers caution that the findings may not apply in the same way to cultures where attitudes towards physical contact and personal space are different.The research was based on survey data and cannot establish cause and effect. It cannot prove that a particular kind of hug creates a lasting memory or that everyone experiences physical affection in the same way. Still, the findings offer a useful way to think about why some ordinary gestures remain important long after the moment has passed. A hug may last only a few seconds, but the feeling of being understood, reassured or supported can become part of how a person remembers that time in their life.You use AI every day. articles.title: Mayors will be free to use share of tax to give residents grants
articles.summary: The Tory Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he's working on what he's calling a "tax rebate scheme".
articles.body:
English regional mayors due to be handed a share of tax revenues by central government will be free to use it to give cash grants to individual residents and businesses, it has emerged.

In his Budget, Chancellor John Healey unveiled plans to allow mayors to keep some cash from income tax and business rates collected locally, describing it as "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham wants local leaders to be given more control over how money is spent in their areas to boost economic growth and services.

But Conservative Tees Valley Mayor Ben Houchen says he has been given assurances that he will be able to give grants to local residents instead.

Lord Houchen told the BBC he is working on a voluntary scheme that would give local residents the opportunity to apply for a share of the tax distributed to his region.

He said Treasury officials had told him this would be acceptable within the government's rules around the devolution of funding.

"It's a technical point around spending decisions," Lord Houchen told the BBC.

He said devolution of funding was a "good thing" and "means mayors are able to decide spending commitments, which includes rebates".

The BBC has been told mayors could choose to use the tax revenues they received from the government to offer grants to individual residents or businesses.

But any mayor who decided to use the money in this way would have less for other local priorities, such as housing and transport.

Lord Houchen has described his proposal as a "tax rebate scheme".

The Treasury would regard these payments as grants, because His Majesty's Revenue and Customs (HMRC) is the only government authority in the UK that can issue income tax rebates.

Most of England's 14 strategic authorities are led by Labour mayors who have welcomed the move to give them a portion of income tax receipts.

Sources close to Reform UK's Greater Lincolnshire Mayor Andrea Jenkyns, and her counterpart in Hull and East Yorkshire, Luke Campbell, say they are waiting for more details to fully understand how they could use these tax revenues to benefit their regions.

The government published its broad approach to reforming funding for local and regional government in England after Wednesday's Budget.

As it stands, mayors of English strategic authorities receive most of their funding from ring-fenced grants, allocated by central government to be spent on specific policy areas.

From April 2028, all mayors of strategic authorities in England will be assigned a share of basic-rate income tax generated in their areas.

Each mayor will receive a bespoke funding allocation that takes into account regional inequalities in tax bases, with the exact amounts to be set at the government's spending review next year.

"The government is not devolving the power to set income tax rates or thresholds to mayors but will be granting significantly more flexibility as to how assigned revenues are spent locally," the government's plan says.

"Mayors will be able to choose where to target funding, for example whether to maintain funding for local transport or prioritise other interventions."

From next year, mayors will also receive a 20% share of locally retained business rates.

This will be the first step towards allowing local and mayoral authorities to retain 100% of their business rates income before the end of the decade.

From 2028, strategic authorities led by mayors will also be given the power to introduce an Overnight Visitor Levy, often dubbed a "tourist tax".

This charge will be an uncapped levy as a percentage of the cost of hotels, bed and breakfasts and other types of accommodation.

Labour mayors in 10 city regions said they would voluntarily limit the charge to 5% , but others - such as Lord Houchen - said they would not introduce the levy.

Burnham - who used to be a mayor himself in Greater Manchester - argues that funding and decision-making powers are too centralised in the UK.

The share of national taxes collected at a local level in the UK is 5.8%, the lowest in the G7, according to the OECD , a global policy forum.

That share is far below that of other countries with large economies such as France (20.4%), Japan (36%) and the US (45.7%).

But critics of fiscal devolution raise concerns about local capability, and inequalities between areas.

The Centre for Cities think tank says some areas may not have the expertise to manage developed powers effectively, risking deeper economic inequalities between areas.

The think tank believes fiscal devolution can offer significant benefits, if the challenges are managed effectively.

The Tees Valley Combined Authority (TVCA) led by Lord Houchen is facing a government inspection into its finances, after Local Government Minister Jim McMahon said he had concerns about its "long-term financial sustainability".

The authority said it welcomed the scrutiny and would continue to make improvements where needed.

articles.title: Ancient account of Jesus challenges centuries of scholarly doubt: 'Totally authentic'
articles.summary: New research on Josephus' disputed passage about Jesus suggests the historian's words were never altered by Christian scribes, a scholar claims. He shared thoughts with Fox News Digital.
articles.body: A scholar believes a nearly 2,000-year-old account of Jesus may be more historically reliable than previously thought, challenging longstanding doubts about one of the earliest non-Christian accounts of his life. T.C. Schmidt, an associate professor of religious studies at Fairfield University in Connecticut, is the author of a 2025 book titled "Josephus and Jesus: New Evidence for the One Called Christ," examining a long-disputed passage about Jesus written by the ancient Jewish historian Josephus. Josephus lived from roughly 37 to 100 A.D. and wrote about Jesus in his work "Antiquities of the Jews," providing one of the few surviving non-Christian accounts of his life. AUTHOR DINESH D'SOUZA CHALLENGES BIBLE SKEPTICS WITH 'STARTLING' ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERIES In the passage, Josephus described Jesus as a wise man who attracted followers and was sentenced to crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. The text also referred to reports that Jesus appeared alive again after his death. For centuries, scholars have debated whether Christian scribes altered the passage, which contains statements about Jesus that some historians believe would have been unusual for a non-Christian Jewish writer. But Schmidt told Fox News Digital that his research suggests the passage is authentic, citing linguistic analysis and comparisons with Josephus' other writings. Schmidt examined ancient versions of Josephus' account in Greek, Latin, Syriac, Arabic and Armenian, using textual comparisons and computer-assisted stylistic analysis to argue that the disputed passage was consistent with Josephus' writing style. ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER MYSTERIOUS FACE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES IN BOOK OF REVELATION CITY His analysis, Schmidt said, found similarities throughout the passage. "I show that every single phrase in the passage can be indexed back to Josephus. It all sounds like something Josephus would say," Schmidt told Fox News Digital. "What this passage does is that it solidifies Jesus in history." Schmidt also argued that some of Josephus' descriptions of Jesus have been misinterpreted, making the passage appear more favorable to Christianity than Schmidt believes Josephus intended. For example, he said Josephus' description of Jesus performing supernatural deeds does not necessarily mean the historian believed those powers came from God. SITE WHERE JESUS WAS CRUCIFIED AND BURIED REVEALS NEW EVIDENCE THAT BACKS BIBLICAL ACCOUNT Instead, the language is more ambiguous, leaving open whether those powers were believed to come from divine or demonic sources. "This actually sounds like something a non-Christian Jew would have said," Schmidt said. "We have other accounts of later Jews saying similar things about Jesus." "So you add it all together and the style of the passage matches Josephus and the claims of the message match what Josephus would have said as a non-Christian Jew," he added. "In other words, the passage looks totally authentic." Schmidt said his findings could strengthen the historical evidence surrounding Jesus' life. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER "What this passage does is that it solidifies Jesus in history," Schmidt said. He said Josephus' account corroborates details found in the Gospels, including Jesus' disciples, his reputation for performing miracles and his crucifixion under Pontius Pilate. Schmidt also emphasized the passage's reference to Jesus' resurrection, arguing that it provides historical evidence of what his earliest followers believed. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "Josephus doesn't himself affirm the resurrection, but he does affirm that early Christians, the disciples of Jesus, believed that Jesus was resurrected on the third day," Schmidt said. When asked about his book's reception, Schmidt said his book has received positive feedback, with some reconsidering their views on the passage's authenticity. Schmidt said his own research led him to question what he had previously been taught. The authenticity of Josephus' account still remains a subject of scholarly debate, with historians continuing to disagree over how much of the passage may have been altered by later Christian scribes. Schmidt also encouraged readers to examine historical sources for themselves, noting that his own research led him to question what he had previously been taught. "I was taught my whole scholarly life that this paragraph by Josephus was not authentic. And I believed that," Schmidt said. articles.title: Difficult negotiations lie ahead in Israel after Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority
articles.summary: Israel’s final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.
articles.body: JERUSALEM — Israel’s final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead. The results released early Friday showed Netanyahu’s bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday’s election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge. “Now comes the truly hard part,” centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: “If you want to know if something’s happening behind the silence you’re hearing now, the answer is yes.” The president will task someone with forming a government Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government? Friday is when much of Israel starts winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them. “There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties,” said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv. The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited. If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario. Netanyahu and Likud target Arab parties without evidence In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had “stolen” the election, potentially with foreign assistance. The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahu’s far-right allies like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats. In Netanyahu’s first public comment Friday, he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties. The head of Israel’s election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said “serious suspicions” of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate. Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu’s party were accusing Qatar of involvement — a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations “ridiculous and dangerous.” As it announced results, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been “entirely unfounded.” “It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population,” he said. By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them. The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to “cast aspersions” on an entire section of the population that “exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.” The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that “allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.” The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week. Opposition could assert control in the upcoming Knesset Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkot’s bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed. Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021. “I believe we should join forces and cooperate with the Arab parties, a legitimate population in the state of Israel,” said Miri Sklair, a resident of Jaffa. If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into security failures before the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

articles.title: Joe Manchin warns Democratic socialists are gaining ground as Democrats remain silent
articles.summary: Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin warns Democratic socialists are gaining ground while longtime Democrats remain silent on the progressive shift.
articles.body: Former West Virginia Sen. Joe Manchin criticized what he sees as his former party's embrace of the progressive left, warning that Democratic socialists are gaining ground while longtime Democrats largely remain silent. "That's why I'm an independent," Manchin said on the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "[Members of the Democratic Party] went from liberal to progressives to DSA. It just keeps going on that trend," he added. KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY Manchin left the Democratic Party after frequently breaking with fellow Democrats while serving in Congress. The longtime moderate registered as an independent in May 2024. In a statement announcing his departure, Manchin criticized extremism on both the left and right, saying he had "seen both the Democrat and Republican parties leave West Virginia and our country behind for partisan extremism while jeopardizing our democracy." Manchin also argued that neither party was willing to "find common ground" or "put country before party." CARVILLE SAYS HE'D RATHER REPUBLICANS KEEP THE HOUSE THAN DEMOCRATS WIN BY FIVE SEATS, HELD 'HOSTAGE' BY DSA During his conversation with Hannity, Manchin expressed disbelief that many Democrats appear unwilling to challenge the Democratic Socialists of America's (DSA) growing influence within the party. "That's beyond me," he said, suggesting that some longtime Democrats may be afraid to challenge the party's more progressive wing. "The bottom line is ... let's look at the elections coming up. If the House changes ... if it flips over to Democrat control, a lot of the flipping is going to happen in kind of a purple area, not a hard blue area. [A] hard blue area is where they're going to maybe flip to DSA." articles.body: Police in Scotland are conducting inquiries into the time former Prince Andrew spent at the king’s private estate at Balmoral with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell, authorities said Friday. Police Scotland said the inquiries were at a “very early stage.’’ “All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries,’’ police said in a statement. “We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further.” Images released earlier this year by the U.S. Department of Justice appeared to show the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, on a shooting trip at the estate with Epstein. Mountbatten Windsor was arrested and held for hours by British police in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office related to his links to Epstein. It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal had been arrested.

articles.title: Spain’s deadly train crash redraws electoral battle lines
articles.summary: The tragedy has upended the November 29 election campaign, shifting attention from housing to security.
articles.body:
A few minutes past 9am on Wednesday, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez posted a message on X declaring there were “lots of reasons to be optimistic about this country”.

His left-wing Socialist Party (PSOE) had sought to seize upon anger over Spain’s housing crisis as a campaign issue ahead of the November 29 election.

Less than an hour later, news of a deadly train crash began to emerge, transforming the campaign. The safety of Spain’s railways, its infrastructure and the government’s ability to deliver essential public services are now key issues after 69 people were killed nine months after a similar disaster.

The mood has changed and Sanchez’s Socialists could be in trouble, analysts say, as the conservative opposition has been handed new grounds to challenge the government on competence and security.

“There are no winners in this tragedy, but it marks a new tone for the campaign where the conservative party could be more comfortable,” said Yolanda Roman, global director for public affairs at ATREVIA, referring to the Popular Party (PP) that has been leading in the polls.

Sanchez’s Socialists were heading for a public debate they could manage, “but after this major tragedy the political framing for the election changed dramatically in all senses”, she added.

PP’s leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo, the prime minister’s main rival, has demanded accountability.

“This is the moment to respect the dead, the injured and their families. That does not mean we will ignore the fact that Spaniards are asking tough questions that demand answers,” he said.

In the wake of the crash, he said the PP would suspend campaign activities for two days.

The far-right Vox leader, Santiago Abascal, who is likely hoping to enter a coalition government with the conservatives, did not show the same restraint.

“We, too, are in mourning – but do not expect us to stay quiet. We will not maintain a complicit silence. It is my duty to denounce Sanchez’s criminal handling of affairs and to work tirelessly so that this coming November 29th … Spain may rid itself of this mafia-like gang,” he said on X.

Hundreds of mostly far-right demonstrators gathered in front of Spain’s Transport Ministry to call for the prime minister’s resignation. “Spain can’t take it anymore,” read a banner.

The political fallout unfolded as questions mounted over what caused the crash .

At 8.53am (7:53 GMT) on Wednesday, a high-speed train travelling from Madrid to Seville slammed into the back of another stationary train on the same track. The incident took place close to Toledo, south of the capital.

Spanish officials pointed to a failure involving the LZB train-control system, which has been used on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line since it opened in the 1990s.

Transport Minister Oscar Puente rejected claims that the accident showed Spain’s railway system was unsafe, describing it as “reliable and safe”, while acknowledging the limits imposed by equipment and human error. His remarks did little to quell the debate over the condition of the country’s rail infrastructure.

Isabel Pardo de Vera, the former president of Adif, the state-owned company responsible for managing Spain’s railway infrastructure, criticised the government over the transition from the older LZB system to the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS). Her comments raised further questions about the pace of modernisation and whether warnings about the network had been adequately addressed.

The crash has revived memories of other fatal accidents. In 2013, 80 people died in a derailment at Angrois, near Santiago de Compostela in the country’s northwest.

Spain’s high-speed rail network has long been regarded as one of the country’s flagship public services, alongside its healthcare system. It carried about 45 million passengers last year, including millions of tourists.

A survey conducted by Spanish media in January, after the previous fatal crash, found that 57 percent of respondents believed rail services had deteriorated since Sanchez took office, while nearly 60 percent said they had little or no confidence in the country’s railway system.

For Sanchez, the timing could not have been worse.

His party has faced corruption scandals involving his inner circle. Separate investigations have targeted Sanchez’s wife, Begona Gomez, over alleged influence-peddling and business corruption, and his brother, David Sanchez, over the circumstances of his public-sector appointment. Both deny wrongdoing.

The government had also been criticised after 80,000 migrants crossed into Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta in late July. The Socialists had faced a backlash from right-wing parties and security personnel over alleged failures to adequately invest in border infrastructure, despite repeated warnings from staff.

And opinion polls have been predicting gains for the far-right Vox party, which lies at the opposite end of the political spectrum.

In late September, images of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal being evicted from her apartment in Madrid went viral.

The episode triggered uproar, channelling discontent over the cost of living and the housing crisis.

Sanchez seized the momentum and called for snap elections: social policy was at the centre of the debate, and the party was hoping to build an electoral campaign. It had even prepared a series of measures dubbed “Social Tuesdays” to make it clear what its agenda was focused on. His campaign was upbeat.

Then the train crash happened, shifting the campaign away from the social issues the PSOE had hoped to highlight.

The government, Roman explained, would now have to spend more time defending its record and answering questions about accountability.

Sanchez hopes to convince an estimated 750,000 undecided left-wing voters of his social agenda, she said.

His PSOE appeared to gain some traction in early October, but was still trailing in most surveys.

The latest polls this week show the Socialists at 26.7 percent, still behind the PP at 31.5 percent. The far-right Vox party remains in third position at 19.1 percent.

articles.title: Can new leaders stop Israel’s slide into isolation?
articles.summary: Americans may not much care who holds power in Jerusalem, but they should.
articles.body:
Israeli voters thronged to the polls in record numbers this week, only to produce a frustratingly murky verdict . It may take weeks of haggling among the country’s fragmented political parties to form a new governing coalition — or to decide the country needs a new election.

Although Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu lost his parliamentary majority , the variable geometry of Israeli politics means he could retain his post, possibly in a new unity government between opposed parties.

Americans may not much care who holds power in Jerusalem, but they should. After all, it was Netanyahu who persuaded President Trump to join Israel’s war to topple Iran’s Islamist regime. The regime remains, but Americans are paying dearly for weapons , gas and diesel as the war drags on.

Also hanging in the balance is America’s historic role as the ultimate guarantor of Israel’s security. After Hamas’s barbaric slaughter of Israeli civilians on Oct. 7, 2023, Americans inevitably drew analogies to the 9/11 massacre and rallied around traumatized Israelis. But Netanyahu’s right-wing government squandered U.S. and international sympathy. The razing of Gaza, the unsettled Iran war and the government’s encouragement of settlers’ aggression and land grabs in the West Bank have drastically deepened Israel’s political isolation.

That is especially true in Europe, where British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband recently declared Israel’s occupation of the West Bank illegal and threatened to impose financial sanctions against settlements.

The one ally Israel can’t afford to lose is the U.S. But the Chicago Council on Global Affairs reported last month that favorable attitudes toward Israel have sunk to historic lows . For the first time, most Americans (56 percent) now favor either cutting or ending U.S. military aid to Israel. A YouGov poll found that 41 percent of Americans — including 62 percent of Democrats — now say Israel is committing genocide in Gaza.

Cratering U.S. support for Israel is driven mainly by Democrats, independents and the young. MAGA Republicans and Christian evangelicals continue to view Israel favorably, although overall Republican support has declined modestly.

When Trump announced his “ Complete and Total ” endorsement of Netanyahu, he wasn’t speaking for most Americans. Fifty-nine percent of voters, including 76 percent of Democrats, express little confidence in Israel’s long-serving leader.

Israel has been sucked into the vortex of America’s tribal politics and Trump’s slumping popularity. No doubt Netanyahu’s assiduous courtship of Trump has helped him score tactical battlefield victories, but the strategic cost is high: the shattering of the bipartisan consensus undergirding America’s staunch support for Israel for nearly eight decades.

Repairing that breach won’t be easy, because young voters especially have soured on Israel. YouGov found that many voters under 30 now sympathize more with Palestinians than Israel (34 percent versus 21 percent), whereas Americans over 65 showed roughly the reverse.

In addition to the Netanyahu government’s self-inflicted wounds, hostility towards Israel — often shading into antisemitism — is percolating on America’s political fringes.

On the extreme right, Tucker Carlson treats his nearly 2 million YouTube subscribers to a tawdry parade of antisemites and Holocaust revisionists such as Nick Fuentes, Candace Owens and Darryl Cooper. Behind a phony pose of fearless inquiry, Carlson deals in conspiracy theories about Jewish control of the U.S. government and hostility to Christians.

Meanwhile, left-wing activists have whipped up a bonfire of anti-Israel bigotry on U.S. campuses.
